questions.title: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization

### Development and types
The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum (central tendon), paired pleuroperitoneal folds, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (crura), and muscular ingrowth from the body wall. Its descent explains the phrenic nerve supply from C3-C5. A simple failure-of-closure account is incomplete: abnormal pleuroperitoneal-fold mesenchyme and disturbed muscle development contribute to the defect; pulmonary hypoplasia may precede and then be aggravated by herniation (dual-hit model).

Bochdalek defects are posterolateral, usually left sided; Morgagni defects are anterior/retrosternal; central tendon defects are uncommon. Eventration is an intact but deficiently muscular diaphragm, rather than a true hole. Distinguish a hiatal hernia through the oesophageal hiatus from CDH. Label the heart, liver, bowel, lung and defect in a schematic.

### Antenatal assessment
Ultrasound shows intrathoracic stomach/bowel, mediastinal shift and a small ipsilateral lung. Assess side, liver position, observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/e LHR), defect severity, associated cardiac/genetic abnormalities and polyhydramnios. Fetal MRI estimates total fetal lung volume and liver herniation. Large defects, liver up, low o/e LHR or lung volume, and major associated anomalies worsen prognosis. Postnatally, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction, oxygen requirement, oxygenation index and ECMO requirement add physiological information. Survival figures must specify whether they describe all diagnosed pregnancies, live births or treated infants.

### Immediate and intensive care management
Plan delivery in a centre with neonatal intensive care and paediatric surgery. Intubate a symptomatic known-CDH neonate and decompress the stomach with an orogastric tube; bag-mask ventilation can inflate intrathoracic bowel. Maintain warmth, analgesia and careful handling. Use gentle pressure-limited ventilation; avoid volutrauma and accept appropriate permissive hypercapnia while following pH, lactate and perfusion. Conventional ventilation is commonly first line; high-frequency ventilation is a rescue option when acceptable gas exchange cannot be obtained within safe pressures. Titrate oxygen to preductal saturation and assess pre/postductal difference. Echocardiography defines pulmonary hypertension and biventricular function; pulmonary vasodilators and vasoactive drugs should follow that physiology, rather than be given automatically.

Give cautious isotonic fluid aliquots with reassessment; excessive fluid worsens pulmonary oedema. Monitor arterial gases, BP, lactate trend, urine output, electrolytes and echocardiography. Refractory cardiopulmonary failure may require ECMO in an eligible infant. Repair follows physiological stabilization, rather than an arbitrary time after birth: acceptable oxygenation/ventilation on stable settings, satisfactory BP and urine output, improving lactate and controlled pulmonary hypertension. Reduce viscera and obtain tension-free closure; use a patch for a large defect. Severe physiology and large defects favour open repair; selected stable infants may undergo minimally invasive repair.

### Sudden acidosis and long-term issues
Check displaced/blocked tube, pneumothorax, worsening pulmonary hypertension, ventricular failure, sepsis, inadequate perfusion and bowel compromise. Check the circuit and tube, examine, obtain bedside imaging/echo and correct the cause promptly. Follow recurrence, pulmonary disease, reflux, growth, hearing and neurodevelopment. The historical shift is from urgent anatomical repair to lung-protective stabilization and delayed repair. FETO is a specialised option for selected severe fetal CDH, with prematurity and balloon-removal risks; it is not routine treatment for every fetus.

### Lung pathology and the management implication
Affected lungs have fewer/smaller airways and alveolar units and a reduced pulmonary vascular bed. Abnormal vascular muscularisation/reactivity contributes to high pulmonary vascular resistance, with right-heart pressure load and possible left-ventricular dysfunction. Consequently, high-pressure ventilation cannot simply 'inflate the missing lung'; overdistension of relatively preserved lung worsens injury and haemodynamics. Gentle ventilation, echocardiography-directed circulation support and delayed repair address this physiological disease alongside the anatomical defect.

![Original teaching schematic: cdh development. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/cdh-development.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [Canadian CDH Collaborative 2023 guideline update](https://fn.bmj.com/content/109/3/239)
- [ERNICA guidelines and endorsed statements](https://www.ern-ernica.eu/guidelines)

questions.title: Paediatric/neonatal fluids, dehydration and electrolyte emergencies
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Paediatric/neonatal fluids, dehydration and electrolyte emergencies

Separate resuscitation, maintenance, pre-existing deficit and ongoing losses; these are not interchangeable. Estimate dehydration from examination and weight change where available. Deficit (mL) = body weight (kg) x percentage dehydration x 10. A 7-kg infant judged 7% dehydrated has an estimated 490-mL deficit; a 10-kg child at 10% has about 1000 mL, but the clinical estimate is imprecise. Severe peritonitis adds third-space losses, sepsis and possible haemorrhage. Use measured clinical response and serial chemistry to refine the plan.

For older infants/children, a common maintenance calculation is 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 for the next 10, and 20 thereafter (the approximate hourly 4-2-1 rule). Neonatal needs differ with age, gestation, humidity, renal function and weight change. Typical term-neonate starting ranges rise from approximately 60-80 mL/kg/day on day 1 to 80-100 on day 2 and 100-120 on day 3; these are starting estimates, not fixed prescriptions for a sick surgical neonate. Prematurity, exposed bowel, phototherapy and losses change requirements. Use glucose-containing maintenance, introduce sodium/potassium according to adaptation, labs and urine output, and avoid blindly applying adult maintenance to neonates.

Shock requires isotonic resuscitation aliquots with frequent perfusion/lung/liver reassessment; choose blood early for haemorrhage. Fluid responsiveness and risk of overload determine further treatment. Replace NG/stoma/urinary losses by measured volume/composition and follow weight, balance, BP, capillary refill, glucose, sodium/potassium/chloride, gases and renal function. Correct hypernatraemic dehydration slowly under close monitoring; avoid rapid osmotic changes. Potassium is added only after renal function/urine output and serum potassium are assessed.

Hyperkalaemia: exclude haemolysed sampling if clinically safe, obtain ECG and assess renal failure, tissue injury, drugs and adrenal disease. Significant ECG changes/severe elevation need monitored IV calcium for membrane protection, insulin with glucose and selected beta-agonist to shift potassium, while stopping potassium input and correcting cause; dialysis may be needed for refractory renal failure. Calcium does not remove potassium. Hypocalcaemia requires ionised calcium interpretation, assessment of magnesium/phosphate and monitored calcium replacement if symptomatic; avoid extravasation and incompatible infusions. State age/weight units explicitly when using a local neonatal emergency-dose protocol.

### IHPS and vomiting-related metabolic abnormalities

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes progressive nonbilious vomiting, dehydration and growth failure, typically in early infancy. Ultrasound evaluates pyloric thickness, channel length and gastric emptying using age/size-aware interpretation; an equivocal examination should not force a diagnosis. Bilious vomiting needs a different urgent pathway.

Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid causes hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; volume contraction activates renin-aldosterone mechanisms, worsening potassium and hydrogen loss. Potassium may initially appear normal despite total-body depletion. The kidney first excretes bicarbonate; with profound chloride/volume and potassium depletion it retains sodium while secreting hydrogen, producing paradoxical aciduria despite systemic alkalosis. Alkalosis can depress ventilation, making anaesthesia unsafe before correction.

Decompress the stomach, use isotonic chloride-containing resuscitation with repeated assessment, then a maintenance/deficit plan with glucose and potassium only after urine output and potassium status are appropriate. Monitor chloride, potassium, bicarbonate, glucose and perfusion; satisfactory hydration, urine output and near-normal acid-base status are prerequisites to pyloromyotomy. It is a medical-resuscitation priority before an elective corrective operation, not an immediate unresuscitated surgical emergency.

Ramstedt pyloromyotomy splits the hypertrophied muscle from gastric to duodenal end while preserving mucosa; ensure an adequate complete myotomy and check for mucosal injury. Open or laparoscopic approaches are acceptable with appropriate expertise. Postoperative vomiting can be transient; persistent symptoms require evaluation for incomplete myotomy, mucosal injury or another diagnosis. Prepyloric vomiting favours acid loss/alkalosis; more distal obstruction can add bile/intestinal fluid losses, dehydration, mixed electrolyte depletion and acidosis if hypoperfusion/sepsis occurs. Do not assume every prolonged upper-GI obstruction has an identical chemistry profile.

### Preoperative correction and operative pitfalls
Review an initially 'normal' potassium with caution: alkalosis and aldosterone-related urinary loss can hide total-body depletion. Chloride replacement restores bicarbonate excretion, while improved perfusion and potassium repletion interrupt the cycle that produces paradoxical aciduria. Use serial venous chemistry/gases, fluid balance and clinical assessment to determine readiness rather than a single fluid bolus. Give appropriate dextrose maintenance for fasting infants and measure glucose; add potassium after urine flow and current chemistry are satisfactory. Local anaesthetic pathways specify exact bicarbonate/chloride targets and should be followed consistently.

A longitudinal myotomy is extended from the antral side to the duodenal end of the hypertrophied muscle, carefully spreading fibres so intact mucosa bulges without injury. The duodenal end is particularly susceptible to perforation; inspect when testing the myotomy. A perforation requires immediate recognized repair and a safe alternative myotomy/recovery plan under the operating team. Incomplete muscle division is a cause of persistent obstruction. Early postoperative feeding is protocol dependent; repeated vomiting with dehydration or failure to improve needs reassessment rather than unlimited reassurance. Include postoperative pain, hydration and follow-up counselling alongside the surgical step.

questions.title: Surgical energy, laser, ultrasonic devices and CUSA
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Surgical energy, laser, ultrasonic devices and CUSA

Monopolar electrosurgery sends current from the active electrode through the patient to a return electrode; it allows cutting/coagulation but risks return-pad burns, coupling and remote thermal injury. Bipolar current passes between two tips, confining the circuit; advanced bipolar devices combine pressure with controlled energy to seal appropriate vessels. Observe each device's vessel-size limit and cooling needs; a seal is not assured merely because tissue was grasped.

Ultrasonic instruments convert high-frequency mechanical vibration into tissue cutting/coaptation with heat; there is no electrical current through the patient, but the blade can remain very hot. They can injure adjacent bowel/ureter/nerve by residual heat. CUSA means Cavitron Ultrasonic Surgical Aspirator: ultrasonic vibration fragments softer tissue with simultaneous irrigation/aspiration, facilitating dissection around firmer vascular/ductal structures, particularly in liver surgery; it does not eliminate bleeding risk. Argon/plasma devices and other ablative instruments have site-specific uses and gas/thermal hazards.

LASER is light amplification by stimulated emission of radiation. Wavelength, absorption, pulse duration and energy density govern penetration and thermal effect. CO2 is strongly absorbed by water and used for superficial precise cutting; Nd:YAG penetrates more deeply; pulsed-dye targets superficial vascular chromophores; holmium is important for endourological stone fragmentation. Applications include airway lesions, selected vascular/skin lesions and endoscopy. Use wavelength-appropriate eye protection, smoke extraction and airway-fire precautions; protect adjacent tissue and avoid claiming all lasers are equally safe for every lesion.

Energy complications include burns, delayed perforation, bleeding from an inadequate seal, smoke exposure, fire and device interaction. Inspect insulation/return electrodes, use the lowest effective energy, maintain visual control and keep heated tips away from vulnerable tissue. A good comparison states mechanism, intended use, advantages and particular limitations, rather than labelling one technology superior in all operations.

### Enteric neuromuscular disorders, appendix reconstruction and manometry

Interstitial cells of Cajal are pacemaker/neuromuscular intermediaries located in defined intestinal plexuses; KIT and ANO1 staining can assist their identification. Motility depends on neurons, smooth muscle and these cells rather than ganglion count alone. Intestinal neuronal dysplasia type B has described submucosal hyperganglionosis/giant ganglia, but diagnostic criteria, age dependence and clinical significance are contested; do not equate every constipation biopsy with a surgical disease. Waardenburg-Shah syndrome combines pigment/hearing abnormalities with Hirschsprung disease, often involving SOX10/EDNRB/EDN3 pathways.

Anorectal manometry records anal resting/squeeze pressures, rectal sensation/compliance and reflexes under a defined technique. Rectal balloon distension normally induces internal-sphincter relaxation (RAIR). An absent RAIR supports investigation for HD or sphincter achalasia but needs technically adequate distension and correlation with biopsy. Sedation, patient age, megarectum and equipment influence results. Uses include refractory constipation, postoperative dysfunction and selected continence assessment; it does not replace anatomy/histology. Distinguish overflow soiling from true sphincter weakness.

The appendix can provide a Mitrofanoff catheterizable urinary channel, a Malone antegrade continence-enema channel, and selected ureteral or other tubular reconstruction. Check length, lumen, mesoappendiceal blood supply and competing needs before using it. A continent channel requires an appropriate valvular tunnel and reliable access; postoperative stomal stenosis, leakage and catheterization difficulty need surveillance. The appendix alone does not solve unsafe bladder storage or a poorly planned bowel-management programme.

### Anorectal manometry: technique and interpretation
Explain the test and perform it with an appropriate catheter, calibrated pressure system and age-specific cooperation/sedation plan. Record baseline anal resting pressure, voluntary squeeze when possible, response to cough/straining and rectal balloon distension in graded safe increments. The internal sphincter contributes much resting tone, while the external sphincter contributes voluntary squeeze. Assess rectal sensation and compliance where cooperation allows; infants cannot provide adult-style sensory thresholds.

RAIR is a transient fall in internal anal-sphincter pressure with rectal distension. An absent reflex can reflect HD, internal anal-sphincter achalasia or technical issues (insufficient distension in megarectum, catheter position, artefact). A preserved reflex makes classic HD less likely but does not explain every constipation cause. Abnormal paradoxical contraction during attempted defaecation may suggest dyssynergia in a cooperative older child; interpret with symptoms and other tests rather than diagnose from a single tracing.

| Finding | Interpretation to investigate |
|---|---|
| Absent RAIR | HD versus sphincter achalasia; verify technique and biopsy |
| Low resting/squeeze pressure | Sphincter weakness/injury or neurological dysfunction |
| High outlet pressure with obstructive symptoms | Functional outlet obstruction; assess anatomy and stool burden |
| Poor sensation/large capacity | Megarectum and altered sensory response, interpreted with age |

Indications include refractory constipation, selected faecal incontinence, postoperative HD/ARM symptoms and assessment before selected bowel-management decisions. The test cannot identify a retained Duhamel spur or establish ganglion status; anatomy and pathology remain separate questions.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA rectosigmoid Hirschsprung guideline (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7318734/)

questions.title: Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter

Complete duplication results from two ureteric buds; incomplete duplication from early division of one bud. By the Weigert-Meyer rule, the upper-moiety ureter generally opens inferomedially and is prone to ectopia/ureterocele or obstruction; the lower-moiety ureter opens superolaterally and is prone to reflux. Exceptions exist. A girl who dribbles continuously despite normal voluntary voiding suggests an ectopic ureter opening below the external sphincter; ordinary enuresis is intermittent. Boys' ectopic ureters usually open above the sphincter and cause infection/obstruction rather than continuous leakage.

Assess ultrasound, urine culture, renal function and moiety function. MR urography maps complex anatomy/ectopic insertion; VCUG evaluates reflux and urethra; DMSA or dynamic imaging measures function, while cystoscopy/vaginoscopy can identify outlets. A poorly functioning upper moiety can be treated by upper-pole heminephrectomy with careful preservation of lower-pole blood supply, or by ureteroureterostomy in suitable anatomy. A functioning moiety favours drainage-preserving reconstruction such as ureteroureterostomy or reimplantation. In the stated example with 3% upper and 36% lower function, do not sacrifice the functioning lower moiety; discuss upper-pole surgery versus drainage reconstruction based on anatomy, infections and tissue quality.

A ureterocele is cystic dilatation of the intravesical distal ureter; developmental theories include persistence of Chwalla's membrane and abnormal ureteral incorporation. Classify intravesical versus ectopic, single versus duplex. Cecoureterocele extends into/beyond the bladder neck. Infection, obstruction or retention may require endoscopic incision/puncture for decompression, followed by assessment for induced/persistent reflux and definitive reconstruction. Preserve functioning moieties and consider the bladder-neck effect.

Megaureter is a dilated ureter, commonly described as over 7 mm; categories are obstructed, refluxing, both, or nonobstructed/nonrefluxing, and primary versus secondary. Assess distal obstruction, VUR, bladder dysfunction and renal function with ultrasound, VCUG when indicated and renography. Many primary nonrefluxing cases improve with observation; recurrent febrile infections, symptoms, worsening dilatation or declining function favour intervention. Definitive reimplantation may require tapering, preserving adventitial blood supply. Temporizing drainage is useful in selected infants.

### Antenatal hydronephrosis, UPJ obstruction and biomarkers

Antenatal urinary-tract dilatation is an imaging finding, not a diagnosis. Record pelvic AP diameter, calyceal involvement, parenchymal thickness/echogenicity, ureter and bladder findings, amniotic fluid and laterality; use a UTD/SFU risk system rather than diameter alone. Consider transient dilatation, UPJ obstruction, VUR, duplex/ureterocele, UVJ obstruction and lower-tract obstruction.

Postnatal ultrasound is generally performed after early physiological dehydration has resolved; severe bilateral disease, solitary kidney or suspected LUTO needs earlier assessment. Evaluate urine infection and renal function in high-risk cases. VCUG is selected for ureteral/bladder abnormalities, suspected outlet obstruction or meaningful reflux risk; it is not obligatory in every isolated mild UPJ dilatation. Diuretic renography assesses differential renal function and drainage when the result affects management. Serial ultrasound and function trends distinguish stable nonobstructive dilatation from progressive obstruction.

Observe asymptomatic stable kidneys with preserved function. Consider pyeloplasty for pain/recurrent infection, progressive dilatation with thinning, impaired differential function or a sustained decline on serial evaluation. A low-function kidney should be judged with anatomy, test reliability, age and contralateral status. Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty excises the narrowed segment, spatulates the ureter and creates a dependent tension-free anastomosis; address a crossing vessel without compromising its supply. Open, laparoscopic or robotic approaches depend on size and expertise. Follow postoperative symptoms, ultrasound and selected functional reassessment.

Urinary NGAL, KIM-1, MCP-1 and other proposed obstruction/fibrosis biomarkers remain adjunctive/research tools; assay variation, infection and age limit specificity. They do not replace ultrasound, functional studies or renal-function monitoring. In PUV, creatinine trend/nadir, BP, proteinuria and established function measures remain clinically important. When discussing recent biomarkers, separate promising association from validated routine decision criteria.

![Original teaching schematic: duplex law. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/duplex-law.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: Testicular descent, impalpable testis and orchidopexy
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Testicular descent, impalpable testis and orchidopexy

Testicular descent has a transabdominal phase influenced by INSL3/gubernacular development and regression of the cranial suspensory ligament, followed by an androgen/genitofemoral-nerve/CGRP-associated inguinoscrotal phase in later gestation. Distinguish undescended, ectopic, retractile, ascending and absent/vanishing testes. Ectopic sites include superficial inguinal pouch, perineum, femoral region and transverse scrotal ectopia.

Examine warm, relaxed children and document testis size/site, scrotum and associated hernia/hypospadias. Routine ultrasound for a nonpalpable testis often fails to locate it and should not postpone specialist assessment. Bilateral nonpalpable testes require prompt endocrine/DSD evaluation, particularly if genital ambiguity or hypoglycaemia/electrolyte abnormalities coexist. AMH/inhibin B and selected hormone tests assess testicular tissue/function; imaging cannot conclusively prove anorchia.

Persistent congenital undescended testis after 6 months corrected age usually needs orchidopexy, completed preferably by 12 months and at latest around 18 months. Hormonal treatment is not a reliable alternative to surgery for inducing descent; fertility-directed hormonal strategies are specialist and not universally adopted. Palpable testes undergo mobilisation, hernia-sac management and tension-free fixation in a subdartos pouch, preserving vas and vessels. Diagnostic laparoscopy for impalpable testes distinguishes intra-abdominal testis, blind-ending vessels and vessels entering the ring, directing further exploration.

A high intra-abdominal testis with insufficient vessel length may need staged Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy: divide testicular vessels and rely on vasal/cremasteric collateral supply, preserving the collateral arcade. A staged approach allows collateral development; traction techniques are alternatives in selected centres. Risks include atrophy, re-ascent, vas injury and hernia. Cryptorchidism increases subfertility, torsion and malignancy risk; early orchidopexy improves surveillance and fertility potential but does not abolish cancer risk.

### Fowler-Stephens selection and follow-up
Before sacrificing testicular vessels, determine whether further mobilisation or a different tension-reducing strategy can achieve safe descent. A low intra-abdominal testis may descend on intact vessels; a high testis more often needs staged collateral-based surgery. Preserve the vasal vascular arcade and avoid collateral injury during later mobilisation. Assess postoperative position and volume; inform families about atrophy, re-ascent and the need for later examination. Retractile testes generally need surveillance for ascent rather than immediate orchidopexy.

### Timeline and signalling
The transabdominal phase is mainly around weeks 8-15; the inguinoscrotal phase is predominantly around weeks 25-35, with variation. INSL3/RXFP2 signalling and gubernacular enlargement are central to the first phase; androgen action, genitofemoral-nerve signalling and gubernacular migration are important later. Testicular descent is a coordinated developmental process, not simply pressure pushing a testis down a canal.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)

questions.title: Lung development, CPAM, sequestration and lobar resection
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Lung development, CPAM, sequestration and lobar resection

### Development and classification
The respiratory diverticulum arises from ventral foregut endoderm; surrounding splanchnic mesoderm forms supporting tissue. Stages are embryonic, pseudoglandular (roughly 5-17 weeks), canalicular (16-26 weeks), saccular (24 weeks to birth) and alveolar (late fetal life through childhood). CPAM is abnormal airway branching/maturation; the older name CCAM should be identified but updated in the answer.

Stocker types: 0, proximal acinar dysplasia; 1, large cysts; 2, multiple smaller cysts and more associated anomalies; 3, microcystic/solid appearing lesions; 4, large peripheral thin-walled cysts. Prenatal imaging also uses macrocystic versus microcystic appearance. Pulmonary sequestration is dysplastic tissue without normal bronchial communication supplied by a systemic artery, usually from the aorta. Intralobar sequestration shares visceral pleura with the adjacent lung; extralobar sequestration has separate pleura and more associated anomalies. Hybrid CPAM/sequestration lesions occur.

### Antenatal and postnatal management
Serial ultrasound documents lesion size, CPAM volume ratio (CVR = length x width x height x 0.52/head circumference), mediastinal shift, hydrops, dominant cyst and systemic supply. A CVR above about 1.6 is a commonly used risk indicator, not a solitary treatment mandate. Assess cardiac compression and fetal growth. Large microcystic lesions with evolving hydrops may be considered for maternal corticosteroids by a fetal team; a dominant macrocyst may be drained with a thoracoamniotic shunt. Selected refractory disease needs specialised fetal intervention. Plan EXIT only when a predicted airway or ventilation problem warrants it.

A distressed neonate needs respiratory support and evaluation for urgent resection. In an asymptomatic infant, cross-sectional contrast imaging defines anatomy and feeding vessels; a normal chest radiograph does not exclude the lesion. Elective resection versus surveillance requires discussion of infection, symptoms, diagnostic uncertainty, rare malignancy concerns and anaesthetic/operative risks. Avoid presenting surgery for all asymptomatic lesions as universally agreed.

### Operative anatomy
The right lung has three lobes and the left two, with a lingula in the left upper lobe. Pulmonary arteries accompany bronchi; veins run mainly in intersegmental planes and drain to the left atrium. At the right hilum, the upper-lobe bronchus is eparterial; the right pulmonary artery lies anterior to the main bronchus. The left pulmonary artery arches above the left main bronchus. Understand individual arterial branches, pulmonary venous drainage and fissural variation before division.

For left upper lobectomy: position and isolate ventilation when feasible; inspect the pleura and fissure; identify and control upper-lobe venous drainage while preserving lower-lobe veins; dissect and divide upper-lobe arterial branches including lingular supply; identify/divide the upper-lobe bronchus without compromising the lower-lobe bronchus; complete the fissure, retrieve specimen, test for air leak and place drainage as indicated. Sequestration requires early recognition and secure control of the systemic feeder. Complications include bleeding, air leak, bronchial injury, infection and residual disease.

### Resection indications and lobar anatomy in an examination answer
Indications for paediatric lung resection include symptomatic congenital malformation, sequestration with infection/complications, localised destructive infection/bronchiectasis, selected tumours and refractory local pathology. The right main bronchus branches to upper-lobe bronchus and bronchus intermedius (middle/lower lobes); the left divides into upper/lower lobar bronchi. Identify superior/inferior pulmonary veins separately and recognise anomalous drainage before division. A posterior left hilar view differs from the familiar anterior 'RALS' relation, so state orientation when drawing.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA guidelines and endorsed statements](https://www.ern-ernica.eu/guidelines)

questions.title: Oesophageal atresia, long-gap reconstruction and substitution
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Oesophageal atresia, long-gap reconstruction and substitution

Gross types are A (atresia without fistula), B (proximal fistula), C (distal fistula; commonest), D (proximal and distal fistulae) and E (H-type fistula without atresia). Disturbed foregut dorsoventral patterning/separation involving pathways such as SHH contributes; a literal failed septum is an oversimplification. Associations include VACTERL (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheo-oesophageal, renal and limb), VACTERL-H (hydrocephalus) and CHARGE (coloboma, heart disease, choanal atresia, growth/developmental problems, genital and ear abnormalities).

Drooling/choking, inability to pass an orogastric tube and a coiled tube on radiograph suggest EA. Abdominal gas implies a distal fistula; a gasless abdomen suggests pure atresia but is not absolute. Protect airway, elevate head, continuously suction the upper pouch with a Replogle tube, avoid feeding and assess cardiac/renal/vertebral anatomy. Bronchoscopy locates fistulae and airway abnormalities when feasible. Prognostic schemes include Waterston (birth weight, pneumonia, anomalies) and Spitz (birth weight below 1.5 kg and major cardiac disease); contemporary outcomes also depend on prematurity and pulmonary status.

Primary repair separates/ligates the fistula and creates a well-perfused tension-conscious oesophageal anastomosis. Thoracoscopy offers improved visualisation and cosmesis in selected stable infants, but requires expertise and vigilance for hypercapnia, acidosis and tension. Open repair remains appropriate for unstable or complex patients. Most contained anastomotic leaks can be managed with drainage, nutritional support, antibiotics as indicated and time; major uncontrolled leaks need individualized revision. Later stricture is treated by controlled endoscopic dilatation; assess reflux and eosinophilic inflammation, with adjuncts/reoperation reserved for refractory cases.

Long-gap EA is defined functionally by inability to obtain a safe primary anastomosis, rather than a universal centimetre cut-off. Preserve native oesophagus when feasible: gastrostomy/nutrition and upper-pouch drainage followed by delayed primary anastomosis, or specialist traction/lengthening approaches. Foker traction may stimulate growth but needs repeated procedures and carries leak, reflux, stricture and intensive-care burdens. Magnamosis uses magnetic compression to join suitable closely apposed pouches; it remains a selected evolving technique, with stricture/reintervention concerns.

Replacement options include gastric pull-up (right gastroepiploic/right gastric supply), gastric tube (usually right gastroepiploic based), colon (selected colic pedicle assessed for continuity) and jejunum (mesenteric arcades, sometimes microvascular augmentation). Routes are posterior mediastinal, retrosternal or selected subcutaneous; posterior is shortest but prior mediastinal scarring/fistula may make alternatives preferable. Ensure vascularity, length without redundancy, tension-free anastomoses and no torsion. Gastric pull-up can cause respiratory compromise, leak, delayed emptying, reflux/dumping and intrathoracic distension; colon can develop redundancy and anastomotic problems; jejunum is peristaltic but technically demanding. Tissue-engineered oesophageal replacements are investigational. Lifelong review addresses swallowing, strictures, reflux, tracheomalacia, recurrent fistula and nutrition.

### H-type fistula and associated anomalies
An H-type fistula can present with coughing/cyanosis during feeds and recurrent respiratory infection despite a patent oesophagus. Contrast studies may miss it; targeted contrast technique and bronchoscopy help locate the tract. Plan cervical versus thoracic exposure by fistula level, divide the connection and close tracheal/oesophageal defects separately with protection of recurrent laryngeal nerves. Evaluate recurrence and airway dysfunction. For long-gap replacement, identify both the conduit blood supply and the route: an excellent conduit can fail from tension, pedicle twisting or a poorly chosen mediastinal passage.

### Spitz groups for the classification subpart
Group I has birth weight at least 1500 g and no major cardiac disease; group II has either weight below 1500 g or major cardiac disease; group III has both factors. These are historical prognostic groups, not indications to withhold repair. Waterston's earlier scheme used weight plus pneumonia/associated abnormalities. Do not attach a historical survival percentage to a contemporary centre without specifying the study era and population.

![Original teaching schematic: ea types. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/ea-types.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA long-gap EA consensus (original publication)](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10098498/)
- [ERNICA guidelines and endorsed statements](https://www.ern-ernica.eu/guidelines)
- [Spitz: Oesophageal atresia at-risk groups (1994)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8078005/)

Check length, lumen, mesoappendiceal blood supply and competing needs before using it. A continent channel requires an appropriate valvular tunnel and reliable access; postoperative stomal stenosis, leakage and catheterization difficulty need surveillance. The appendix alone does not solve unsafe bladder storage or a poorly planned bowel-management programme.

### Anorectal manometry: technique and interpretation
Explain the test and perform it with an appropriate catheter, calibrated pressure system and age-specific cooperation/sedation plan. Record baseline anal resting pressure, voluntary squeeze when possible, response to cough/straining and rectal balloon distension in graded safe increments. The internal sphincter contributes much resting tone, while the external sphincter contributes voluntary squeeze. Assess rectal sensation and compliance where cooperation allows; infants cannot provide adult-style sensory thresholds.

RAIR is a transient fall in internal anal-sphincter pressure with rectal distension. An absent reflex can reflect HD, internal anal-sphincter achalasia or technical issues (insufficient distension in megarectum, catheter position, artefact). A preserved reflex makes classic HD less likely but does not explain every constipation cause. Abnormal paradoxical contraction during attempted defaecation may suggest dyssynergia in a cooperative older child; interpret with symptoms and other tests rather than diagnose from a single tracing.

| Finding | Interpretation to investigate |
|---|---|
| Absent RAIR | HD versus sphincter achalasia; verify technique and biopsy |
| Low resting/squeeze pressure | Sphincter weakness/injury or neurological dysfunction |
| High outlet pressure with obstructive symptoms | Functional outlet obstruction; assess anatomy and stool burden |
| Poor sensation/large capacity | Megarectum and altered sensory response, interpreted with age |

Indications include refractory constipation, selected faecal incontinence, postoperative HD/ARM symptoms and assessment before selected bowel-management decisions. The test cannot identify a retained Duhamel spur or establish ganglion status; anatomy and pathology remain separate questions.

### Hirschsprung disease: diagnosis, pull-through and postoperative obstruction

### Pathogenesis, genetics and diagnosis
Failure of neural-crest-derived enteric cells to populate distal bowel produces contiguous distal aganglionosis of submucosal and myenteric plexuses. The affected segment fails to relax, with proximal dilatation. RET-pathway abnormalities are central; EDNRB, EDN3, SOX10 and other genes contribute. Associations include Down syndrome, Waardenburg-Shah syndrome and Mowat-Wilson syndrome. Genetic counselling is especially relevant in familial, syndromic and long-segment disease.

Presentations include delayed meconium, neonatal obstruction, enterocolitis, failure to thrive or childhood constipation. Rectal examination may produce explosive stool but is neither necessary nor confirmatory. Contrast enema can show a transition zone, reversed rectosigmoid ratio and delayed evacuation; it may be misleading in neonates and total colonic disease. Anorectal manometry demonstrates an absent rectoanal inhibitory reflex (RAIR), but histology establishes the diagnosis.

Take adequate rectal suction biopsies above the physiologically hypoganglionic anal zone, with sufficient submucosa; a full-thickness biopsy is used when suction tissue is inadequate or results conflict. H&E assesses absent ganglion cells and hypertrophic nerves. Increased acetylcholinesterase activity supports diagnosis; absent mucosal/submucosal calretinin staining is useful. Interpret with specimen quality, age and expert pathology. Intraoperative biopsies must demonstrate ganglionated bowel clear of the transition zone.

### Definitive operation
Decompress with rectal irrigations, correct sepsis/nutrition and map the disease. Selected stable, decompressed rectosigmoid cases can have a single-stage transanal endorectal pull-through; diversion is appropriate for instability, severe enterocolitis, difficult decompression or extensive disease. Swenson removes the aganglionic rectum with a low anastomosis; Soave pulls ganglionated bowel through an endorectal muscular cuff; Duhamel creates a retrorectal pull-through and joins it to the retained anterior rectum. Preserve sphincters and dentate-line sensation; avoid twist, tension, ischaemia and a restrictive cuff.

Total colonic aganglionosis requires serial biopsies including small bowel; imaging alone cannot define its proximal extent. Emergency diversion must be placed in proven ganglionated bowel. Definitive ileoanal pull-through options include straight/Soave-type or modified Duhamel reconstruction, chosen with nutritional and continence implications. Follow hydration, growth, sodium loss, skin injury and enterocolitis. “Ultra-short segment” disease is controversial: distinguish internal anal sphincter achalasia (absent RAIR with ganglion cells) and functional constipation before proposing resection.

### Persistent symptoms after surgery
First distinguish true incontinence from overflow due to obstruction. Obtain operative/histology records, examination under anaesthesia, contrast enema, and repeat biopsy when indicated. Mechanical causes include stricture, twisted pull-through, retained Soave cuff or Duhamel spur; histological causes include transition-zone pull-through/residual aganglionosis. Functional causes include internal sphincter achalasia and dysmotility. Treat demonstrable structural disease appropriately; use irrigations, a structured bowel regimen and selected botulinum toxin injection for outlet dysfunction. Redo surgery needs a defined cause and experienced team. Long-term surveillance covers continence, constipation, HAEC, psychosocial health and transition to adult care.

![Original teaching schematic: pullthrough. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/pullthrough.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [ERNICA rectosigmoid Hirschsprung guideline (2020)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7318734/)

questions.title: Non-Wilms renal tumours and small-round-cell diagnostics
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Non-Wilms renal tumours and small-round-cell diagnostics

Infant renal masses include congenital mesoblastic nephroma (CMN), Wilms tumour, rhabdoid tumour and less commonly other lesions. CMN is common in early infancy; classic and cellular forms have different biological behaviour, with ETV6-NTRK3 fusions characteristic of many cellular lesions. Nephrectomy with complete excision is usual management; selected higher-risk/recurrent cellular disease needs oncology treatment and molecularly directed options. Monitor recurrence according to pathology/stage rather than assuming every CMN is benign.

Clear-cell sarcoma of kidney is aggressive and can metastasise to bone and brain; BCOR alterations support diagnosis in many cases. Treat with complete surgical staging and protocol-specific multiagent chemotherapy/radiotherapy. Rhabdoid tumour often affects infants and shows loss of SMARCB1/INI1 expression (or less commonly SMARCA4 abnormalities); search for synchronous CNS disease and predisposition. Pediatric RCC occurs more in older children, including translocation-associated forms; treatment differs from Wilms chemotherapy.

Immunohistochemistry is interpreted as a panel alongside morphology, site, age and molecular tests. Examples: RMS desmin/myogenin/MyoD1; neuroblastoma neuronal/neuroendocrine markers and PHOX2B; Ewing sarcoma CD99/NKX2.2 with a defining fusion test; lymphoma lineage markers; rhabdoid INI1 loss; germ-cell tumours SALL4 and subtype markers; hepatoblastoma hepatocytic markers with other morphology-specific stains. A marker is not perfectly specific, so avoid diagnosing a 'small round blue cell tumour' from CD99 or desmin alone.

Molecular tests can establish fusions, refine risk and identify actionable targets, using FISH, RT-PCR or sequencing as appropriate. Obtain tissue with a planned biopsy route and enough material for histology and ancillary testing; avoid necrotic tissue and inappropriate decalcification. Communicate treatment history because preoperative chemotherapy changes tumour composition. Liquid biopsy of circulating tumour DNA/cells is promising for residual disease and genomic profiling but remains tumour- and assay-specific, and cannot universally replace tissue.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NCI PDQ: Wilms and other childhood kidney tumours](https://www.cancer.gov/types/kidney/hp/wilms-treatment-pdq)

questions.title: Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia and Kasai outcomes
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia and Kasai outcomes

### Recognition and investigation
Conjugated jaundice is pathological. Persistent jaundice, pale/acholic stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly warrant prompt direct bilirubin measurement and hepatobiliary assessment. A direct bilirubin above 1 mg/dL is an important abnormal threshold; the older requirement that it exceed 20% of total bilirubin can miss disease. Differential diagnosis includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, infection, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Alagille syndrome, metabolic/endocrine disorders, genetic bile-transport disease and parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis.

Assess stool colour, growth, bleeding and splenic/associated abnormalities. Tests include fractionated bilirubin, liver enzymes/GGT, albumin, glucose, INR (including response to vitamin K), CBC, cultures when needed and targeted metabolic/genetic investigations. Fasting ultrasound assesses gallbladder morphology, triangular-cord sign, ducts, cysts and vascular anatomy. No single negative ultrasound or scintigraphic result reliably excludes BA. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy can demonstrate excretion; absent excretion is nonspecific and must not delay definitive evaluation. Liver biopsy often shows bile duct proliferation, bile plugs, portal oedema and fibrosis. Intraoperative cholangiography establishes extrahepatic patency/anatomy when BA is suspected.

### Pathology and operation
BA is progressive fibro-obliterative cholangiopathy with interacting developmental, inflammatory and immune mechanisms. CMV-associated BA is a described subgroup; association does not prove CMV causes all BA, and antiviral treatment needs specialist selection. Anatomical types are I (common bile duct), II (common hepatic duct, with subtypes), and III (at porta hepatis; most common). A cystic hilar lesion may represent cystic BA rather than a patent choledochal cyst; assess distal patency and hepatic ducts.

Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy removes the fibrotic extrahepatic remnant and exposes microscopic ductules at the portal plate, connected to a Roux-en-Y jejunal limb. Earlier diagnosis and surgery improve the chance of bile drainage; age is not the sole criterion. Avoid damage to portal vessels and inappropriate deep excision. Provide high-energy nutrition, fat-soluble vitamins, cholangitis treatment and surveillance. The benefit of routine steroids is unsettled and protocol dependent.

### Prognosis and transplantation
Jaundice clearance and bilirubin after Kasai, age/fibrosis at operation, anatomical/syndromic disease, recurrent cholangitis, centre experience and portal hypertension influence native-liver survival. Some children retain native liver long term, while others develop cirrhosis despite initial bile drainage. Follow growth, fat-soluble vitamins, coagulopathy, varices, ascites, hepatopulmonary syndrome and malignancy surveillance where indicated. Refer early for transplant assessment after failed drainage, progressive decompensation, refractory portal-hypertension complications, severe growth failure or recurrent uncontrollable cholangitis. Kasai is a bridge to long-term native-liver health or transplantation, rather than a guaranteed cure.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN infant cholestasis guideline](https://www.naspghan.org/files/documents/pdfs/position-papers/Guideline_for_the_Evaluation_of_Cholestatic.23.pdf)
